subject: korean
topic: Ordering food: counting words and prices
title: Does the bill match the order?
goal: Check a short ordering dialogue against a menu, find the first line whose amount does not match, and design orders of your own that fit a fixed budget.
thinking: Checking a statement against given facts
Finding where a mistake starts and what it passes on
Producing several different orders that meet the same limits
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to read prices aloud or repeat '주세요' sentences. Here you audit what the clerk says against the menu, notice that one wrong amount makes the next amount wrong too, and design orders yourself.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows the counting words 한, 두, 세 ... with 개 and 잔
Can read prices written like 3,000원
material:
A small cafe has this menu (원 = won, the Korean money).
커피 한 잔: 3,000원
빵 한 개: 2,000원

손님 = customer, 직원 = clerk. Read the dialogue.

손님: 커피 두 잔 주세요.
직원: 네. 커피 두 잔, 6,000원이에요.
손님: 그리고 빵 세 개 주세요.
직원: 네. 빵 세 개, 5,000원이에요.
직원: 모두 11,000원이에요.

steps.prompt: Which line is the FIRST one whose amount does not match the menu?
lines: 손님: 그리고 빵 세 개 주세요.
steps.explain: Line 4 is the first mistake: 빵 is 2,000원 each, so three breads are 6,000원, not 5,000원. Line 2 is fine (two coffees at 3,000원). Line 5 adds line 2 and line 4 correctly, but it starts from the wrong bread amount, so it is wrong too; it is not a separate mistake.
hints: Take one item at a time: find its price on the menu, then compare it with the amount the clerk says.
Check the 커피 line first to see what a correct line looks like, then check the 빵 line in the same way.

steps.prompt: The customer is going to pay the amount in the last line. What should the clerk's last line have said?

options.reveals: This comes from checking each item against the menu first and only then putting the amounts together.
You may have read 세 개 as 두 개. Compare the number the customer said with the number you used.
This repeats the clerk's own amounts. The sum is fine, but one of the amounts it is built from is not.

steps.explain: Coffee 2 x 3,000 = 6,000 and bread 3 x 2,000 = 6,000, so the total is 12,000원. The clerk's 11,000원 is a correct sum of a wrong bread amount.
hints: Work out the right amount for each item separately.
Then compare the whole with the 11,000원 on the bill.

steps.prompt: You have exactly 13,000원 and want to spend all of it on 커피 (c cups) and 빵 (b pieces). Order at least one of each and at most 6 items in all. Find two different orders.

constraints.ok: Whole numbers, at least one of each.
constraints.fail: Use whole numbers, and at least one cup and one piece.
That is more than 6 items in all.
The bill is not 13,000원 (커피 3,000원 each, 빵 2,000원 each).

steps.explain: Two orders work: 커피 1 + 빵 5 (3,000 + 10,000) and 커피 3 + 빵 2 (9,000 + 4,000). With 커피 2 the bill is 12,000원, and 커피 5 already costs more than 13,000원 together with one bread.
hints: Choose how many coffees first, then see how much money is left for bread.
If the money left is not a multiple of 2,000, change the number of coffees.

steps.prompt: Say one of your orders to the clerk, in Korean. Use both items, their counting words, and 주세요.

checks.label: has a number with 잔/개 (한 잔, 두 개 ...)

selfAssess: Does my order use the numbers of one of my two orders from the previous step?
Does 커피 go with 잔 and 빵 with 개?
Would the clerk know exactly what to bring?

modelAnswers.text: 커피 한 잔, 빵 다섯 개 주세요.
커피 세 잔하고 빵 두 개 주세요.
modelAnswers.note: Uses 하고 to join the two items.

badAnswers.why: No amount and no 빵.

badAnswers.text: 커피 세 잔, 빵 두 개.
badAnswers.why: Names the items and amounts but is missing 주세요.

steps.humanReview: Whether the amounts in the sentence match an order that really costs 13,000원, and whether the counting words are natural.
hints: Say the coffee part first, then the bread part, then finish with 주세요.
Count coffee with 잔 and bread with 개.

rubric.full: Names line 4 and says 3 breads at 2,000원 are 6,000원, not 5,000원
rubric.partial: Names the final total only, without tracing it back to line 4
rubric.none: Names no line or a line whose amount is right

rubric.full: Both orders cost exactly 13,000원 and obey the item limit

alternatives: Naming line 5 is understandable because it also differs from the right total (12,000원). The stronger answer sees that it repeats the wrong bread amount from line 4.
A student may guess the clerk misheard 세 as 두. That could explain the mistake, but the amount is still wrong for what the customer said.
hardCases: If the bread price were different today, 5,000원 could be right. The task fixes the menu as printed.
The line alone cannot show whether the clerk got the price or the count wrong, only that the amount does not fit.

cautions.language: Counting words (한 잔, 세 개) are native Korean numbers; the prices are written in digits and need no Sino-Korean reading.
cautions.culture: Ordering at the counter and saying the total aloud is common in cafes. The menu and prices are invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Prices are digits; they are read aloud as 삼천 원 (3,000), 이천 원 (2,000), 육천 원 (6,000), 만이천 원 (12,000).

auto: The two orders and the 13,000원 / 6-item limits (s3)
Surface features of the spoken order (s4)
human: Whether the spoken order is natural and matches one of the student's own orders

subject: korean
title: Who is the teacher in this class?
goal: Narrow down who is the teacher from short self-introductions, notice when a new sentence clashes with your answer, and write a sentence that repairs the clash.
thinking: Combining several short clues
Revising a conclusion when new information arrives
Handling clues that cannot all be true
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to fill in 이에요 or 아니에요. Here you use the sentences as clues, change your answer when a clue arrives, and decide what to do when a clue contradicts the others.
prerequisites: Can read Hangul
Knows 저는 ~이에요 and ~이/가 아니에요
Knows the words 학생, 선생님, 한국 사람, 미국 사람
material: Three people are in a Korean class: 민호, 에밀리 and 켄. One of them is the teacher; the other two are students. Each person has only one nationality (한국 사람 = Korean, 미국 사람 = American). Everybody tells the truth in the first two clues. The clues arrive one by one.

steps.prompt: After each clue, choose the most reasonable thought.

options.text: It is either 민호 or 켄.
options.reveals: Sees that one 'is not' removes one person and keeps the others open.

options.text: It is 켄; 민호 did not speak.
options.reveals: Treats 'not 에밀리' as 'must be 켄' although nothing is said about 민호.

options.text: It is 에밀리; she spoke first.
options.reveals: Misses 아니에요, which means 'is not'.

stages.after: 아니에요 removes 에밀리 only. Both 민호 and 켄 are still possible.

stages.info: 켄: 저는 미국 사람이에요. 선생님은 한국 사람이에요.

options.text: 켄
options.reveals: Overlooks that 켄 says the teacher is Korean while he is American.

options.text: 에밀리
options.reveals: Goes against the first clue.

options.text: 민호
options.reveals: Puts clue 1 (not 에밀리) together with clue 2 (the teacher is Korean, 켄 is American).

stages.after: The teacher is Korean, 켄 is American and 에밀리 said she is not the teacher, so 민호 is left.

stages.info: 민호: 저는 한국 사람이에요. 저는 학생이에요.
stages.ask: What is the most reasonable thing to do now?

options.text: Keep 민호 as my best guess, but ask him again.
options.reveals: Keeps the best-supported answer but lowers confidence and checks the source.

options.text: The clues cannot all be true. I would check what each person really said.
options.reveals: Sees that the four sentences clash, so some sentence must be wrong or misunderstood.

options.text: 켄 is the teacher after all. His nationality does not matter.
options.reveals: Throws away a clue because it is in the way.

stages.after: If everybody is truthful, nobody can be the teacher: 에밀리 is not, 켄 is not Korean, and 민호 says he is a student. So a sentence is wrong or was misunderstood. Asking again, or keeping 민호 with less confidence, are both fair; ignoring a clue is not.

steps.reflect: The first clue removed one person, the second chose one, and the third contradicted the choice. A clash between clues is also information: it tells you to check the sentences instead of picking the answer you like.
hints: Before choosing, say in your own words what each sentence rules in or rules out.
After each new clue, check whether it agrees with everything you already know.

steps.prompt: Write one Korean sentence that 민호 could say instead of '저는 학생이에요', so that all the clues agree and he is the teacher.

checks.label: does not deny being the teacher or say he is a student

selfAssess: Does my sentence make 민호 the teacher?
Does it still agree with 민호 being Korean and with the other clues?

modelAnswers.text: 저는 선생님이에요.
저는 한국 사람이에요. 선생님이에요.
modelAnswers.note: Repeats his nationality, then the new fact.

badAnswers.why: The same sentence that caused the clash.
Says the opposite of what is needed.

steps.humanReview: Whether the sentence is natural; short answers like 저는 선생님이에요 are fully acceptable.
hints: Which word in 민호's last sentence clashes with the other clues?
Replace only that word and keep the ending 이에요.

rubric.full: Says which people each clue removes and which are left
rubric.partial: Reaches the right person without saying why

rubric.full: Says the clues cannot all be true and what to check, or keeps 민호 with lower confidence
rubric.partial: Notices something is odd but does not say what to do

alternatives: In stage 3, both 'ask 민호 again' and 'recheck every sentence' are good moves. In stage 2 a student may note 에밀리's nationality is unknown; it does not matter because she is already ruled out.
The repair sentence could also change 켄's or 에밀리's line; the task asks about 민호 only.
hardCases: A person could have two nationalities in real life. The task says each person has only one.
If a speaker is allowed to lie, no answer can be proved. The task states that the first two clues are truthful.

cautions.language: 이에요 and 아니에요 are spelled and pronounced with a final 에요; the negative has the subject marker 이/가 (선생님이 아니에요).
cautions.culture: Names are common Korean/English names; 'American' and 'Korean' are only used as simple labels.
cautions.accessibility: No images. All clues are plain text sentences with the speaker's name first.

auto: Surface check that the sentence says 선생님이에요 and avoids 아니/학생
human: Whether the reasoning about the clash is sensible

subject: korean
topic: Giving reasons with -아서/어서 and clock times
title: Is one reason enough?
goal: Test a stated reason (-아서/어서) against clock times, revise your view when a second fact appears, and write the full set of reasons in Korean.
thinking: Testing a reason against times
Asking what would have happened without the reason
Revising a judgement when a new fact appears
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to join two sentences with -아서/어서. Here you decide whether a reason really explains what happened, and what changes when another reason appears.
prerequisites: Knows clock times (6시 10분) and past tense -았/었어요
Knows 기다렸어요, 걸려요, 늦었어요
Has seen -아서/어서 for reasons
material:
서연 went to see a film. 영화는 7시에 시작했어요 (the film began at 7:00). 서연이 친구에게 말했어요: “지하철이 안 와서 늦었어요.”

서연의 이야기:
- 6시 10분에 집에서 나갔어요. 역은 집 바로 앞이에요.
- 역에서 지하철을 20분 기다렸어요.
- 지하철은 보통 40분 걸려요.
- 극장은 지하철역 바로 앞이에요.

steps.prompt: Using only these facts, how good is the reason “지하철이 안 와서 늦었어요”?

options.text: Not good: leaving home at 6:10 was already too late for a 7:00 film.
options.reveals: Does not add up the ride: 6:10 plus 40 minutes is 6:50, in time.

options.text: Good: without the wait she would have arrived at 6:50, in time.
options.reveals: Compares what happened with what would have happened without the reason.

options.text: Cannot say: the facts do not tell how long the ride takes.
options.reveals: Overlooks that '보통 40분 걸려요' gives the usual ride time.

steps.explain: She left at 6:10, waited 20 minutes (6:30) and rode 40 minutes, so she arrived at 7:10, 10 minutes late. Without the wait she would have arrived at 6:50, before 7:00. So the wait fully explains her lateness here.
hints: Write the clock time after each part of her trip: leaving, waiting, riding.
Then redo the trip once without the waiting part and compare with 7:00.

steps.prompt: New information: 그날 지하철은 사고 때문에 천천히 가서 55분 걸렸어요. 서연은 7시 25분에 도착했어요. Now how good is the reason “지하철이 안 와서 늦었어요”?

options.text: Still the whole reason: the wait explains all of the 25 minutes.
options.reveals: Keeps the first answer without re-checking the times.

options.text: Wrong: the slow train is the only reason she was late at all.
options.reveals: Throws the wait away; without the slow train she would still arrive at 7:10, late.

options.text: Only part: without the wait she would still arrive at 7:05.
options.reveals: Redoes the times with the new facts and compares both reasons.

steps.explain: 6:10 + 20-minute wait + 55-minute ride = 7:25. Without the wait the arrival would be 7:05, still 5 minutes late; without the slow train it would be 7:10, still 10 minutes late. Both facts matter, so one reason alone does not explain the lateness.
hints: Redo the clock times with the 55-minute ride.
Take away the waiting once, then take away the slow ride once, and compare each arrival with 7:00.

steps.prompt: Write in Korean what 서연 should have told her friend so that both reasons are included. Use -아서/어서 (or -고, -니까).

checks.label: mentions the slow ride (천천히 / 사고 / 오래)

selfAssess: Did I include both the wait and the slow ride?
Does each reason connect to being late, not just sit next to it?
Would my friend understand why she arrived at 7:25?

modelAnswers.text: 지하철을 20분 기다려서 늦었어요. 그리고 사고 때문에 지하철이 천천히 가서 오래 걸렸어요.
지하철이 안 와서 20분 기다렸어요. 또 지하철이 천천히 가서 늦었어요.

badAnswers.why: Gives only the first reason.
Gives only the second reason and leaves out the wait.

steps.humanReview: Whether the two reasons are linked to the lateness in natural Korean, and whether the connector fits the meaning.
hints: Write one sentence for the waiting and one for the slow ride.
End at least one of them with 늦었어요.

rubric.full: Compares the real arrival with the arrival without the reason, in both steps
rubric.none: Accepts or rejects the reason without times

rubric.full: Changes the verdict in step 2 and says why the wait is only part of the story
rubric.partial: Changes the verdict without a reason

alternatives: In step 2 a student may say 'the wait still matters, but it is not the whole reason'. That is the intended idea in other words.
A student may add a third reason (not leaving earlier). That is fine; the task fixes the departure time but leaving earlier would also have helped.
hardCases: Whether 5 or 10 minutes late counts as 'late' depends on the cinema; the task counts any minute after 7:00 as late.
If the cinema is not exactly at the station, the times change. The task fixes it as right in front of the station.

cautions.language: -아서/어서 gives a reason, but it cannot be followed by -ㅂ시다 or -(으)세요; the task only asks for statements.
cautions.culture: Arriving after a film has started is a minor problem in many places; no cultural knowledge is needed beyond that.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Times are written in words and digits (6시 10분 = 6:10).

auto: Surface checks of the written reasons
human: Whether the written reasons are natural and complete

subject: korean
topic: Giving and following directions on a subway line
title: Which stop is 'the third stop'?
goal: Decide what a friend's directions leave open, use new messages to narrow the possibilities, and ask the missing questions in Korean.
thinking: Finding missing information in directions
Narrowing possibilities with new facts
Asking questions that get the missing facts
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to follow a clear route. Here the route is incomplete: you find what is missing and ask for exactly that.
prerequisites: Knows 타세요 / 내리세요 and 세 번째
Knows 쪽 (direction) and 앞 (in front of)
Can read a list of stations in order
material:
민아 is going to 지우's school by subway. Line 2 stops in this order, from left to right:
가역 - 나역 - 다역 - 라역 - 마역 - 바역 - 사역
민아's home is next to 라역, so she gets on at 라역. 지우 sends two messages. They arrive one by one.

steps.prompt: After each message, choose the most reasonable thought.

stages.info: 지우: 2호선을 타세요. 세 번째 역에서 내리세요.
stages.ask: Can 민아 be sure where to get off?

options.text: Yes: 'the third stop' names only one station.
options.reveals: Counts in one direction only and forgets that the line goes both ways.

options.text: No: the message does not say which way to ride.
options.reveals: Sees that the third station to the left and to the right are different stations.

options.text: No: the message does not say what time the train comes.
options.reveals: Looks for a detail that cannot change which station is the third.

stages.after: If 라역 itself is not counted, the third station is 가역 on the left and 사역 on the right. The direction is missing.

stages.info: 지우: 사역 쪽으로 가는 지하철을 타세요.
stages.ask: Which station is 'the third station' for 민아, who gets on at 라역?

options.reveals: Starts counting with the next station after the one she boards.
Counts the boarding station as the first.

options.text: I cannot be sure: it depends on whether 라역 itself is counted.
options.reveals: Sees that there are two ways to count and neither is stated.

stages.after: Many speakers do not count the station where you get on, which gives 사역; some do count it, which gives 바역. Choosing 사역 is a good guess, and being unsure is also reasonable. The safest move is to ask.

stages.ask: What does this tell you about how 지우 counted?

options.text: 지우 counted 라역 as the first station.
options.reveals: If that were so, the third station would be 바역, not the school's station.

options.text: The place of the school says nothing about the counting.
options.reveals: The school's station is what shows which count gives the right stop.

options.text: 지우 did not count 라역, the station where you get on.
options.reveals: Uses the school's station to decide between the two ways of counting.

stages.after: The school is at 사역. Only counting 마역 (1), 바역 (2), 사역 (3) reaches it, so 지우 did not count the boarding station.

steps.reflect: The first message left the direction open, the second left the counting open, and the third settled the counting. Notice that each answer was safe only as long as you said what you did not yet know.
hints: Write the stations on a line and mark 라역. Count to the third station on each side.
Before choosing, ask yourself what 지우 would have to add to make only one station possible.

steps.prompt: At the start, 민아 had only the first message. Write the Korean question(s) she could send so that she gets both missing facts.

checks.label: asks about the direction (쪽 / 방향 / 어느)
asks about the counting (번째 / 포함 / 세어)

selfAssess: Do my questions get the direction?
Do they get how the stations are counted?
Could 지우 answer each one with a short reply?

modelAnswers.text: 어느 쪽으로 가는 지하철을 타요? 라역도 세어요?
사역 쪽으로 가요? 세 번째 역은 라역부터 세는 거예요?
modelAnswers.note: Names a direction guess, then the counting.

badAnswers.why: Asks only about the direction.
Asks about the number but not the direction.

steps.humanReview: Whether the questions are polite and natural enough to send to a friend.
hints: Write one question for each missing fact.
Use the words 쪽 and 번째 if they help.

rubric.full: Names both the direction and the counting as open
rubric.none: Names neither or an unrelated detail

rubric.full: Asks for both facts in clear questions

alternatives: In stage 2, 'cannot be sure' is as good as '사역'. A student who picks 바역 only has counted the boarding station; the stage text points out why that is the less common count.
The question in step 2 may be asked in two messages or in one.
hardCases: Some speakers really do count the boarding station. That is why stage 2 does not say 'only 사역'.
In real cities the direction is named by the last station or the line colour, not only by a station on the line.

cautions.language: 쪽 means 'side/direction'; 번째 turns a number into 'the nth'. Both are usually taught with the counting words in the same unit.
cautions.culture: In Korean subways, directions are given by the end station of a direction (like 사역 방면), which is why 지우 says 사역 쪽. The station names here are invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The line is given as a text list from left to right, and the task never needs the picture.

auto: Surface check that the questions ask about the direction and the counting
human: Whether the questions are natural, polite and clear

subject: korean
title: Make three sentences true at once
goal: Decide whether two sentences fix an order, find every order that fits three sentences, and say what is certain and what is left open.
thinking: Checking whether information is enough
Finding several answers under constraints
Explaining what is fixed and what is free
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to fill in 전에 or 후에. Here you work out what the sentences do and do not fix, and you build the orders yourself.
prerequisites: Knows -기 전에 and -(으)ㄴ 후에 (before / after)
Can read short sentences about daily routines
material:
하준 describes his weekday morning. He does four things, each once, one after another: 운동 (exercise), 샤워 (shower), 아침 (breakfast), 출근 (leaving for work). He says three things:
① 샤워하기 전에 운동해요.
② 아침을 먹은 후에 출근해요.
③ 운동을 한 후에 아침을 먹어요.

steps.prompt: Use only ① and ②. Is it certain that 운동 comes before 출근?

options.text: No: ① and ② are separate pairs; nothing links them.
options.reveals: Checks which events each sentence actually connects.

options.text: Yes: 운동 is mentioned first, so it happens first.
options.reveals: Takes the order of the words in the story for the order of the events.

options.text: Yes: people shower before work, so 운동 is earlier too.
options.reveals: Brings in an everyday habit instead of using only the sentences.

steps.explain: ① only says 운동 is before 샤워, and ② only says 아침 is before 출근. Neither sentence connects the two pairs, so 운동 could even come after 출근 in the sentences alone. ③ will connect them.
hints: Draw each sentence as two boxes with an arrow from the earlier event to the later one.
Check whether any box appears in both drawings.

steps.prompt: Now use ①, ② and ③. Give the position of each activity (1 = first, 4 = last) in an order that makes all three sentences true. Find two different orders.

constraints.ok: All positions are whole numbers from 1 to 4.

constraints.fail: Each position from 1 to 4 must be used exactly once.

constraints.ok: ① 샤워하기 전에 운동해요 is true.
constraints.fail: ① is not true: 운동 must be before 샤워.

constraints.ok: ② 아침을 먹은 후에 출근해요 is true.
constraints.fail: ② is not true: 아침 must be before 출근.

constraints.ok: ③ 운동을 한 후에 아침을 먹어요 is true.
constraints.fail: ③ is not true: 운동 must be before 아침.

steps.explain: Three orders work: 운동-샤워-아침-출근, 운동-아침-샤워-출근 and 운동-아침-출근-샤워. In all of them 운동 is first. Only the place of 샤워 is free, as long as it is after 운동.
hints: Start with the activity that has to be before both of the others it is linked to.
Place 샤워 last and see whether the other three sentences still hold.

steps.prompt: In one or two sentences (English or Korean): what do ①, ② and ③ settle for certain, and what do they leave open?

checks.label: says what is fixed or open (first, any place, possible ...)

selfAssess: Did I say which event is certainly first?
Did I say which event can move?
Is my reason based on the sentences, not on habit?

modelAnswers.text: 운동은 항상 첫 번째예요. 샤워는 운동 후라면 두 번째, 세 번째, 네 번째 어디든 가능해요.
Exercise must be first because it is before both the shower and breakfast. The shower can be second, third or last.

badAnswers.why: No event named.
Lists the events but says nothing about what is fixed or open.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reason given for 'exercise is first' and 'the shower is free' really follows from ①, ② and ③.
hints: Look at your orders: which activity is in the same place every time?
Which activity changes place?

rubric.full: Says ① and ② do not link the two pairs
Gives two correct, different orders
rubric.none: Gives orders that break a sentence

rubric.full: Says 운동 is always first and 샤워 is free after it, with a reason

alternatives: All three valid orders count; a student may find only two.
The explanation may be given in a table or arrows in words (운동 → 샤워) instead of full sentences.
hardCases: The story says each activity happens once, one after another. If two could happen at the same time (e.g., eating while exercising), the task would have more answers.
'-고 나서' or '-는 동안' would change the meaning; the task uses only 전에 and 후에.

cautions.language: -기 전에 attaches to the LATER event's verb stem (샤워하기 전에 = before showering), while -(으)ㄴ 후에 attaches to the EARLIER event (먹은 후에). This often confuses learners.
cautions.culture: A morning routine with exercise and breakfast is a common topic; the routine is invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Positions 1-4 are numbers; the order can be said aloud as 'first, second, third, fourth'.

auto: The positions in s2 (all three sentences, each position used once)
human: Whether the final explanation is correct and based on the sentences

subject: korean
topic: Time words and verb endings in a diary
title: A diary with a date problem
goal: Find the diary sentence whose time word and verb ending clash, decide which repairs are possible, and write your own matched sentences.
thinking: Checking a text against a given calendar
Seeing that more than one repair can be right
Producing matched time words and endings
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to put a verb into the past or future. Here you check an existing text against a calendar, repair it in more than one way, and write your own.
prerequisites: Knows past -았/었어요 and future -(으)ㄹ 거예요
Knows 어제, 오늘, 내일, 모레, 지난, 이번, 다음
Knows the weekdays
material:
Today is 수요일 (Wednesday), 9 p.m. 마리 writes in her diary. This week: 월요일 (Mon), 화요일 (Tue), 수요일 (Wed, today), 목요일 (Thu), 금요일 (Fri).

1. 어제는 화요일이어서 학원에 갔어요.
2. 오늘은 수요일인데 아침부터 비가 오고 있어요.
3. 내일은 목요일이라서 친구를 만날 거예요.
4. 지난 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 볼 거예요.
5. 모레 금요일에는 일찍 잘 거예요.

steps.prompt: Which line has a time word and a verb ending that do not fit each other?
lines: 오늘은 수요일인데 아침부터 비가 오고 있어요.
지난 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 볼 거예요.
steps.explain: Line 4 has 지난 금요일 ('last Friday', already past) with 볼 거예요 (future). Line 1: 어제 = Tuesday, past ending. Line 2: today, in progress. Line 3: 내일 = Thursday, future. Line 5: 모레 = the day after tomorrow = Friday, future.
hints: For each line, find the time word and say whether it is before, during or after Wednesday evening.
Then look at the verb ending of each line and compare.

steps.prompt: Which repairs of line 4 give a correct sentence? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 지난 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 봤어요.
options.reveals: Keeps the time word 'last Friday' and changes the ending to the past.

options.text: 지난 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 보고 싶어요.
options.reveals: Changes the ending to a wish, but a wish does not fit a day that is over.

options.text: 이번 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 볼 거예요.
options.reveals: Keeps the future ending and changes the time word to the coming Friday.

options.text: 어제 금요일에는 친구와 영화를 봤어요.
options.reveals: Fixes the ending but 어제 is Tuesday, not Friday.

steps.explain: Either the ending or the time word can change. 'Last Friday ... went' or 'this coming Friday ... will go' are both correct; which one Mari meant is a question to ask her.
hints: Decide first: is it the verb ending or the time word that you want to change?
After a repair, check the sentence against the calendar again.

acceptable.reason: One valid repair (changing the ending) is enough if you say the other is also possible.
One valid repair (changing the time word) is enough if you say the other is also possible.

steps.prompt: Write three short Korean sentences about your own days: one about yesterday (어제), one about today (오늘) and one about tomorrow (내일). Match each verb ending to its day.
selfAssess: Does each sentence use the ending that fits its day?
Did I use all three time words?
Could someone check my sentences against a calendar?

modelAnswers.text: 어제는 친구를 만났어요. 오늘은 학교에 가요. 내일은 일찍 일어날 거예요.
어제 영화를 봤어요. 오늘은 집에서 쉬어요. 내일 운동할 거예요.

badAnswers.text: 어제 영화를 볼 거예요. 오늘 쉬어요. 내일 갈 거예요.
badAnswers.why: The first sentence has 어제 with a future ending.

steps.humanReview: Whether each ending really matches its time word. The surface checks only see that a past and a future ending are somewhere in the text.
hints: Write the time word first, then pick the ending that fits it.
Read each sentence once more and ask: has this already happened?

rubric.full: Picks line 4 and says why (past time word, future ending)
Sees that either the ending or the time word can change
rubric.none: Gives a repair that is still wrong

rubric.full: All three sentences fit their time words
rubric.none: More than one does not fit

alternatives: Naming line 4 as 'the time word is wrong' or 'the verb is wrong' are both fine; it is the pair that clashes.
Line 2 uses -고 있어요 for something that is going on in the evening; this is correct, not an error.
hardCases: 지난 금요일 could mean 'Friday of last week', and 이번 금요일 'Friday of this week'. Some speakers use 지난 for the latest Friday that has passed. The task relies on the calendar above (today is Wednesday).
A sentence like 내일 만났어요 would be wrong in plain statements, but 내일 is fine with a story told in the past, such as in a novel.

cautions.language: Dates and tense are linked, but Korean has no 'will'; the future form -(으)ㄹ 거예요 shows plan or guess.
cautions.culture: Writing a diary at the end of a day is a common school habit in Korea; the diary is invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The week is given as a list of five days in words.

auto: Surface features of the three sentences (s3)
human: Whether each sentence's ending fits its time word and sounds natural

subject: korean
title: Passing on the leader's message
goal: Find the relayed sentences that do not report what the leader said, separate a wrong form from a wrong meaning, and relay a new message yourself.
thinking: Checking a retelling against the original
Telling a changed form from a changed meaning
Producing a faithful retelling
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to turn quoted speech into -대요 or -래요. Here you check a ready-made retelling against the original, find what changed, and relay a new message.
prerequisites: Knows reported-speech endings -(느)ㄴ대요, -(이)래요, -(으)래요
Knows -지 않아도 되다 (no need to) and -지 마세요
Reads short workplace messages
material:
팀장님 (the team leader) told 민수 four things in the hallway:
“내일 회의는 오후 3시예요. 장소는 5층 회의실이에요. 자료는 오늘까지 보내 주세요. 점심은 먹지 않아도 돼요.”
민수 now passes the four things on to 수아, who was not there.

민수: 내일 회의는 오후 3시래요.
민수: 장소는 5층 회의실이래요.
민수: 자료는 오늘까지 보냈대요.
민수: 점심은 먹지 말래요.

steps.prompt: Which of 민수's lines do NOT report what 팀장님 said? Pick one of them.
steps.explain: Lines 3 and 4 both change the message. Line 3: 보냈대요 says the materials were already sent, but 팀장님 asked for them to be sent (보내래요). Line 4: 먹지 말래요 says 'told us not to eat', but 팀장님 only said eating is not necessary (안 먹어도 된대요). Lines 1 and 2 are faithful.
hints: For each original sentence, decide: is 팀장님 stating a fact, or asking someone to do something?
Then check whether the ending of the retold line is a statement ending or a request ending.

steps.prompt: Which are faithful ways to pass on the fourth sentence, 점심은 먹지 않아도 돼요? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 점심은 먹지 말래요.
options.reveals: Turns 'no need to eat' into 'told us not to eat', which is a different message.

options.text: 점심은 안 먹어도 된대요.
options.reveals: Keeps 'no need' and marks the words as someone else's.

options.text: 점심은 안 먹어도 돼요.
options.reveals: Drops the sign that these are 팀장님's words, so it sounds like your own permission.

options.text: 점심은 먹지 않아도 된다고 해요.
options.reveals: Keeps the meaning and marks it as reported with -다고 해요.

steps.explain: -대요 is the short form of -다고 해요, so b and d say the same thing. a changes the meaning, and c leaves out who said it.
hints: Say the original meaning in English first: 'it is not necessary' or 'it is forbidden'?
Look for the version that keeps that meaning AND shows that someone else said it.

acceptable.reason: Valid. The long form -다고 해요 in d is equally faithful.
Valid. The short form -대요 in b is equally faithful.

steps.prompt: 팀장님 sends one more message: “회의가 4시로 바뀌었어요. 늦지 마세요.” Write what you would say to 수아 to pass it on, in Korean.

checks.label: marks the words as reported (-대요, -래요, -다고 해요 ...)
passes on the request about 늦

selfAssess: Did I keep both parts: the new time and the request?
Did I change the request ending (-세요) into a reported ending?
Does it sound like I am passing it on, not giving my own order?

modelAnswers.text: 회의가 4시로 바뀌었대요. 늦지 말래요.
팀장님이 회의가 4시로 바뀌었다고 해요. 그리고 늦지 말라고 하셨어요.
modelAnswers.note: Long forms and the leader named.

badAnswers.why: Copies the leader's words; nothing marks them as reported.
Reports the time but leaves out the request.

steps.humanReview: Whether the reported forms are used correctly (statement vs request) and whether the tone to 수아 is natural.
hints: Split the message into a statement and a request.
Choose a reported ending for each one.

rubric.full: Names line 3 or 4 and says what the original meant
rubric.partial: Names a line without saying what changed

rubric.full: Sees that line 3 has the wrong kind of ending and line 4 has the wrong meaning
Both parts relayed with reported endings

alternatives: In s2, choosing only b or only d is acceptable: the two forms are equal.
A student may relay the time as 4시로 바뀌었다는 거예요; this is also fine.
hardCases: 보냈대요 can be correct if 팀장님 had said 자료를 보냈어요. The task relies on the original sentence 보내 주세요.
Some speakers use 먹지 말래요 for 'it is better not to eat'. The task's original says only 'not necessary'.

cautions.language: -대요 / -래요 / -재요 are contractions of -다고 해요 / -라고 해요 / -자고 해요 and are mostly spoken. For a request the ending is -(으)래요; for a statement it is -(느)ㄴ대요 or -(이)래요.
cautions.culture: Relaying messages from a superior to a colleague is everyday workplace talk; the names are invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. All four relays are plain text and are numbered 1-4 by the line picker.

auto: Surface check for reported endings, 4시 and 늦 (s3)
human: Whether the relayed message keeps the meaning and sounds natural

subject: korean
topic: Did it happen? (-ㄹ 뻔했다, -는 바람에, -ㄹ까 봐, -ㄹ 줄 알았는데)
title: Who failed the test?
goal: Decide from four sentences who definitely failed a test, say what you would ask where the sentence does not settle it, and write your own pair of sentences.
thinking: Telling what a sentence entails from what it only suggests
Seeing when the information is not enough
Producing sentences with a near-miss ending
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives the meaning of each ending. Here you use the endings as evidence about what happened and say what a sentence leaves open.
prerequisites: Knows -ㄹ 뻔했다 (almost), -는 바람에 (because of, with a bad result)
Knows -ㄹ까 봐 (for fear that) and -ㄹ 줄 알았는데 (thought that ... but)
Knows 붙다 (pass) and 떨어지다 (fail) for exams
material:
Four people talk about their driver's-licence test (운전면허 시험). 붙다 = to pass, 떨어지다 = to fail an exam.

지민: 긴장하는 바람에 운전면허 시험에 떨어졌어요.
서준: 운전면허 시험에 떨어질 뻔했는데 겨우 붙었어요.
도현: 붙을 줄 알았는데 떨어졌어요.
하은: 운전면허 시험에 떨어질까 봐 열심히 연습했어요.

steps.prompt: Who definitely failed the test? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 지민
options.reveals: Reads -는 바람에 as a bad result that really happened.

options.text: 하은
options.reveals: Takes a worry (떨어질까 봐) for a result.

options.text: 서준
options.reveals: Reads 떨어질 뻔했다 as 'failed', but 뻔했다 means it nearly happened and did not.

options.text: 도현
options.reveals: Reads 붙을 줄 알았는데 as an expectation that turned out wrong.

steps.explain: 지민 failed (떨어졌어요). 도현 expected to pass but failed (떨어졌어요). 서준 only almost failed and then passed (겨우 붙었어요). 하은 says what she feared, not what happened.
hints: For each person, find the verb that says whether they passed or failed.
Check if the verb is about the result, or about a worry or an almost.

acceptable.reason: 지민 is a definite failure; 도현 also failed, so add them for the full set.
도현 is a definite failure; 지민 also failed, so add them for the full set.

steps.prompt: You want to know whether 하은 passed. Which question would settle it?

options.text: 연습은 매일 했어요? 몇 시간 했어요?
options.reveals: Asks about something already said in the sentence.

options.text: 시험은 봤어요? 결과는 어때요?
options.reveals: Sees that her sentence may be from before the test.

options.text: 시험이 많이 어려웠어요?
options.reveals: Takes it for granted that she has taken the test.

steps.explain: 하은's sentence shows a worry and her practice. It does not say whether she took the test yet, or what the result was, so the question has to ask for both.
hints: Read 하은's sentence again: does it say that the test is over?
Which question would give you the result, even if the test is still ahead?

steps.prompt: Write two Korean sentences about driving tests, one where someone failed because of something unwanted (-는 바람에 or 떨어졌어요), and one where someone almost failed but passed (-ㄹ 뻔했다).

checks.label: a failure sentence (바람에 / 떨어졌 / 불합격 / 못 붙)
mentions the test or passing (시험 / 붙 / 합격)

selfAssess: Does my first sentence say that the person really failed?
Does my second sentence say that they almost failed but did not?
Are the two endings used in the right way?

modelAnswers.text: 너무 긴장하는 바람에 시험에 떨어졌어요. 이번에는 떨어질 뻔했는데 겨우 붙었어요.
시험에 떨어졌어요. 하지만 지난번에는 떨어질 뻔했는데 붙었어요.

badAnswers.why: Only the near-miss; there is no sentence where the person really failed.
Only the failure; there is no near-miss sentence.

steps.humanReview: Whether the near-miss sentence really means 'almost but did not', and whether the failure sentence is natural.
hints: Write the failure sentence first and end it with a past verb.
For the near miss, use the verb stem + -ㄹ 뻔했는데 and say what happened in the end.

rubric.full: Picks 지민 and 도현 and says why 서준 and 하은 are not definite failures
Asks for the test and its result
rubric.partial: Asks about only one of them

rubric.full: Both sentences have the right meaning

alternatives: In s1, choosing only 지민 or only 도현 is valid but incomplete.
In s2 a student may ask 시험 결과가 나왔어요? alone; this is also a good question.
hardCases: 도현's sentence does not say what he did next. Failing is the natural reading of 붙을 줄 알았는데 떨어졌어요, which says 'failed' directly.
하은 could have passed or failed; the task treats her sentence as not settling it.

cautions.language: -ㄹ 뻔했다 always means 'it did not happen'. Learners often read it as 'it happened'.
cautions.culture: A licence test with a written and a road part is common; no cultural knowledge is needed.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The four people are shown as four lines in text.

auto: Surface check of the two written sentences
human: Whether the sentences are natural and use the endings correctly

subject: korean
title: Is the summary fair?
goal: Check whether a '-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다' summary really follows from the numbers before it, decide which summaries of one case are fair, and write your own.
thinking: Checking a summary against numbers
Judging which approximations are fair
Producing a summary that follows from given facts
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to fill in -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 with its meaning. Here you test whether the summary is justified by the figures and which ways of rounding are fair.
prerequisites: Knows -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 ('it amounts to')
Can use -씩 for 'each' and 남짓 / 조금 넘게 for 'a little over'
Knows 1시간 = 60분
material:
Four people summarise their practice with -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 ('it comes to ...'). Each summary should follow from the numbers before it. (1시간 = 60분)

1. 매일 30분씩 일주일 동안 걸었으니까 모두 세 시간 반을 걸은 셈이에요.
2. 하루에 20분씩 6일 연습했으니까 한 시간 연습한 셈이에요.
3. 일주일에 세 번, 한 번에 40분씩 수영하니까 한 주에 두 시간 수영하는 셈이에요.
4. 하루에 두 시간씩 5일 공부했으니까 열 시간 공부한 셈이에요.

steps.prompt: Which summary does NOT follow from its numbers?
lines: 매일 30분씩 일주일 동안 걸었으니까 모두 세 시간 반을 걸은 셈이에요.
하루에 20분씩 6일 연습했으니까 한 시간 연습한 셈이에요.
일주일에 세 번, 한 번에 40분씩 수영하니까 한 주에 두 시간 수영하는 셈이에요.
하루에 두 시간씩 5일 공부했으니까 열 시간 공부한 셈이에요.
steps.explain: Line 2: 20분 x 6일 = 120분 = 2시간, not 한 시간. Line 1: 30분 x 7 = 210분 = 3시간 반 (correct). Line 3: 40분 x 3 = 120분 = 2시간 (correct). Line 4: 2시간 x 5 = 10시간 (correct).
hints: Take one line at a time and test whether its total really follows from its own numbers.
Use the same unit for the numbers and for the total before you compare.

steps.prompt: Someone exercises 일주일에 네 번, 한 번에 50분씩. Which summaries are fair? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 일주일에 거의 다섯 시간 운동하는 셈이에요.
options.reveals: Rounds 3 hours 20 minutes far up; '거의 다섯 시간' is about 4 h 40 min or more.

options.text: 일주일에 세 시간 남짓 운동하는 셈이에요.
options.reveals: Sees 200 minutes as a little over three hours.

options.text: 일주일에 세 시간 조금 넘게 운동하는 셈이에요.
options.reveals: Says the same as 남짓 with different words.

options.text: 일주일에 두 시간 반 운동하는 셈이에요.
options.reveals: Takes off 50 minutes; 2.5 hours is 150 minutes.

steps.explain: 4 x 50 = 200분 = 3시간 20분, which is a little over 3 hours (세 시간 남짓 / 조금 넘게). 거의 다섯 시간 is 300분 and 두 시간 반 is 150분, both far off.
hints: Express the weekly time in one unit first.
Then ask of each option: is the figure it names close to that time?

acceptable.reason: Fair. The wording in c means the same.
Fair. The wording in b means the same.

steps.prompt: Write your own summary with -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이에요: give a rate with -씩 or 한 번에 ..., a number of days or times, and the total that follows.

checks.label: gives a rate (-씩 / 마다 / 한 번에)

selfAssess: Does the total in my summary follow from my own numbers?
Did I check the calculation before writing the total?
Is 셈이에요 the right ending for 'it amounts to', not just 'I did it'?

modelAnswers.text: 하루에 30분씩 4일 걸었으니까 모두 두 시간 걸은 셈이에요.
일주일에 두 번, 한 번에 45분씩 수영하니까 한 주에 한 시간 반 수영하는 셈이에요.

badAnswers.why: No rate and no numbers; it does not say what it amounts to.
Has the numbers but no 셈이에요 and no total.

steps.humanReview: Whether the calculation behind the written total is correct. The surface checks cannot do arithmetic.
hints: Pick simple numbers first, such as 30분 x 4일.
Do the calculation on the side, then write the sentence with the total.

rubric.full: Finds line 2 and gives the right total (2시간)
Picks the two fair summaries and rejects the two far-off ones
The total follows from the numbers
rubric.partial: The sentence is well formed but the total is wrong

alternatives: In s2, 'a little over three hours' or 'about 3 hours 20 minutes' are both fair summaries.
A student may point out that line 4 is exact, so 셈이다 is not needed; the task treats it as correct.
hardCases: '거의 네 시간' for 3시간 20분 is borderline: it is 40 minutes short. The task does not use it as an option.
셈이다 is sometimes used when the amounts are exactly equal. Both uses are fine here.

cautions.language: -(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 means 'it amounts to'; it is not the same as -(으)ㄹ 셈이다 ('I intend to'). The task uses only the 'amounts to' meaning.
cautions.culture: Walking, swimming and studying with the number of days are everyday topics; no cultural knowledge is needed.
cautions.accessibility: No images. All numbers are written in digits and in Korean number words; the calculation can be done with the numbers read aloud.

auto: Surface checks of s3 (셈이, a rate, numbers)
human: Whether the total in the student's sentence is correct and the sentence is natural

subject: korean
title: Is pricier always better?
goal: Judge how well a '-(으)ㄹ수록' claim fits a table, build counterexample pairs from the table, and reword the claim so that it fits the data.
thinking: Testing a general claim against data
Building counterexamples that meet exact conditions
Rewording a claim to the strength the data supports
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to complete '-(으)ㄹ수록 ... -아/어지다'. Here the sentence is a general claim: you test it on data, find the cases that break it, and rewrite it.
prerequisites: Knows -(으)ㄹ수록 ('the more ... the more ...')
Knows 대체로, 항상, 꼭 and negative endings
Can compare two numbers in a table
material:
A blogger writes: “커피는 값이 비쌀수록 만족도가 높다.” (-(으)ㄹ수록 = the more ..., the more ...). A survey of six cafes gave this table. 만족도 = satisfaction score out of 10. The cafes are numbered from the cheapest (1) to the most expensive (6).

번호 1: 3,000원, 만족도 6점
번호 2: 4,000원, 만족도 8점
번호 3: 5,000원, 만족도 7점
번호 4: 6,500원, 만족도 9점
번호 5: 8,000원, 만족도 6점
번호 6: 9,000원, 만족도 8점

steps.prompt: How well does the blogger's sentence fit the table?

options.text: Not for every pair, but the dearer three score a bit higher.
options.reveals: Compares pairs and the overall pattern separately.

options.text: It fits: for any two cafes, the more expensive one scores higher.
options.reveals: Looks at the general direction of the table only and skips the individual pairs.

options.text: It is reversed: for any two cafes, the cheaper one scores higher.
options.reveals: Notices a few cheaper-and-better pairs and turns them into a rule.

steps.explain: Some pairs agree with the claim (1 and 2), some break it (2 and 3, 4 and 5). The three dearer cafes average about 7.7 points and the three cheaper ones 7.0, so a weak trend exists, but the claim does not hold for every pair.
hints: Pick two cafes at random and check which one is dearer and which scores higher.
Do this for a few pairs before you decide.

steps.prompt: Find two counterexamples: pairs of cafes where cafe a is cheaper than cafe b, but cafe b has a LOWER score than cafe a. Enter the two cafe numbers.

constraints.ok: Both are cafe numbers from 1 to 6.
constraints.fail: Use whole cafe numbers from 1 to 6.

constraints.ok: Cafe a is cheaper than cafe b.
constraints.fail: Cafe a must be the cheaper one (a smaller number).
The dearer cafe must score LOWER than the cheaper one.

steps.explain: Five pairs break the claim: (2,3), (2,5), (3,5), (4,5), (4,6). For example, 번호 2 costs 4,000원 and scores 8, but the dearer 번호 3 (5,000원) scores only 7. Pairs with equal scores (such as 2 and 6) are not 'higher' either, but they are not listed here.
hints: Choose a cafe with a high score and look at the dearer cafes after it.
Is there a dearer cafe with a lower score?

steps.prompt: Rewrite the blogger's sentence in Korean so that it fits the table better.

checks.label: weakens or limits the claim (대체로, 항상 ... 아니다, 편이, 예외 ...)
is still about price and satisfaction (비싸 / 값 / 가격 and 만족)

selfAssess: Is my sentence no stronger than what the table shows?
Does it still say something about price and satisfaction?
Could a reader find a counterexample to my new sentence in the table?

modelAnswers.text: 비싸다고 해서 항상 만족도가 높은 것은 아니에요.
대체로 비쌀수록 만족도가 높은 편이지만 예외도 있어요.
modelAnswers.note: Keeps the trend and admits the exceptions.

badAnswers.why: The same claim, unchanged.
No limit and nothing about price.

steps.humanReview: Whether the new sentence is as strong as the table supports, no more and no less.
hints: Add a word that shows the claim is not true for every pair.
Or turn the sentence around: 'being dearer does not always mean ...'.

rubric.full: Compares pairs and also sees the overall pattern
rubric.partial: Sees only the pairs or only the pattern
rubric.none: Accepts or rejects the claim without pairs

rubric.full: Both pairs are correct and different
Weakens the claim to what the table supports
rubric.partial: Weakens it too far or not enough

alternatives: Other counterexamples are equally valid: (2,5), (3,5), (4,6).
A student may reword the claim as a comparison of two groups (the dearer half scores higher on average), which also fits the table.
hardCases: Pairs with equal scores (2 and 6, 1 and 5) are not counterexamples to 'higher', but they are not examples of the claim either. The task asks for pairs with a lower score so that nobody has to decide.
Six cafes are a small sample; any trend is weak evidence.

cautions.language: -(으)ㄹ수록 describes a trend ('the more ... the more'), and the blogger uses it as if it were true of every pair.
cautions.culture: Prices are invented; blogging about cafes is common in Korea but needs no background.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The table is given as six lines of text.

auto: The two pairs in s2 (the expression language checks price order and scores)
Surface check for a limited claim about price and satisfaction
human: Whether the reworded claim is neither too strong nor too weak

subject: korean
topic: Scope of negation with 모두 ... -지 않다
title: The notice with two readings
goal: Find what a notice says for sure under both of its readings, update your view as facts arrive, find attendance numbers that fit, and rewrite the notice so that only one reading remains.
thinking: Seeing that a sentence can have two readings
Keeping the safe conclusion and narrowing it with facts
Rewriting to remove an ambiguity
differsFromPlain: Plain practice translates a sentence with 모두 and -지 않다. Here the sentence has two readings; you decide what both readings share, what each new fact rules out, and how to write each reading clearly.
prerequisites: Knows 모두 (all) and 아무도 / 한 명도 (nobody)
Knows negative -지 않다 and the formal -습니다 style
Can read a short notice
material:
A club has 10 members. The club rule (in English): a meeting can be held only if at least 6 of the 10 members come. A notice was posted after the meeting day:
“오늘 회의에는 회원이 모두 참석하지 않았습니다.”
The sentence can be read in two ways. Reading A: no member came. Reading B: not every member came (some came, some did not). Facts arrive one by one.

steps.prompt: After each piece of information, choose the most reasonable thought.

stages.info: The notice above is all you know.
stages.ask: What can you be sure of under BOTH readings?

options.text: Nobody attended.
options.reveals: Picks reading A as if it were the only one.

options.text: At least one member was absent.
options.reveals: Finds what both readings share: A and B both leave someone out.

options.text: Exactly half of the members attended.
options.reveals: Adds a number that the notice does not give.

stages.after: Under A everyone was absent and under B some were absent, so 'at least one member was absent' is true in both. Nothing else is certain yet.

stages.info: Everybody agrees that the club president (회장) was at the meeting.
stages.ask: Which reading is now ruled out?

options.text: Both readings are still possible.
options.reveals: Does not use the new fact.

options.text: Reading B: some came and some did not.
options.reveals: The president being there fits B, so B is not ruled out.

options.text: Reading A: no member came.
options.reveals: Uses the fact that a member came to rule out 'nobody came'.

stages.after: If the president came, 'no member came' is false. Reading B, 'some came, some did not', remains.

stages.info: 회의는 열리지 못했습니다. (The meeting could not be held.)
stages.ask: How many members came, using the club rule?

options.text: Between 1 and 5 members.
options.reveals: Combines 'at least one' with 'fewer than six'.

options.text: Between 6 and 9 members.
options.reveals: Forgets that the meeting needs at least 6 to be held.

options.text: No member (0).
options.reveals: Forgets the president was there.

stages.after: At least 1 came (the president) and fewer than 6 (otherwise the meeting could be held), so 1 to 5.

steps.reflect: The first answer was safe because it held in both readings. Each new fact removed one possibility and let you be more exact. You did not need to guess the writer's reading to say what is certain.
hints: Ask what is true in Reading A and what is true in Reading B, then keep only what is true in both.
After each fact, check which reading it contradicts.

steps.prompt: Give two possible attendance counts that fit all three facts: x members came and y members were absent (10 members in all).

constraints.ok: x and y add up to the 10 members.
constraints.fail: x and y must add up to 10.

constraints.ok: At least one member (the president) came.
constraints.fail: At least one member came (the president).

constraints.ok: Fewer than 6 came, so the meeting could not be held.
constraints.fail: 6 or more would have been enough to hold the meeting.

steps.explain: Any x from 1 to 5 works (with y = 10 - x). 0 is excluded because the president came, and 6 or more is excluded because the meeting was not held.
hints: Start from the lowest and the highest number that the facts allow.
Then check the total with y.

steps.prompt: Rewrite the notice in Korean twice: one sentence that can mean only 'no member came', and one that can mean only 'not every member came'.

checks.label: a version that means nobody came (한 명도 / 아무도 ...)
a version that means not everybody came (모두 ... 것은 아니 / 일부 ...)

selfAssess: Does my first sentence mean only that nobody came?
Does my second sentence mean only that some did not come?
Would a reader still be unsure about either?

modelAnswers.text: 회원이 한 명도 참석하지 않았습니다. 회원이 모두 참석한 것은 아닙니다.
아무도 참석하지 않았습니다. 일부 회원만 참석했습니다.

badAnswers.why: The original notice, still ambiguous.
Gives only one of the two versions.

steps.humanReview: Whether each version really has only one reading, and the formal style is natural.
hints: For 'nobody', use a word meaning 'not even one'.
For 'not everybody', say who did come or that 'it is not that all came'.

rubric.full: States what holds under both readings and why
rubric.partial: States the safe conclusion without why
rubric.none: Picks one reading as if it were the only one

rubric.full: Rules out the reading that the new fact contradicts
rubric.partial: Rules out the right reading without a reason

rubric.full: Both versions have a single meaning

alternatives: In stage 1, a student may say 'both readings are possible, so I can only say someone was absent'. This is the same idea as option b.
Other clear versions are 전원이 불참했습니다 (nobody came) and 일부 회원이 불참했습니다 (some did not come).
hardCases: Many readers hear 모두 ... -지 않았습니다 as reading B. Stress and context can make it reading A, and writing does not show stress.
모두 참석하지는 않았습니다 (with 는) leans to reading B but is not completely safe.

cautions.language: The negation can cover 'all' (not all came) or the verb (all did not come). With 모두 in front, Korean often leaves both open; stress and context decide.
cautions.culture: Club notices after a meeting are everyday; the club and the rule are invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The two readings are named in words (A and B) in the material.

auto: The choices in the three stages
Surface checks of the two rewritten sentences
human: Whether each rewritten sentence has exactly one reading

subject: korean
topic: Cause and contrast connectors in a news summary
title: The connector that points the wrong way
goal: Find a summary sentence whose connector claims more than the report, choose connectors that do not, and write a contrast sentence of your own.
thinking: Checking a connector against the facts
Choosing among connectors with different strength
Producing a connected pair of sentences
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks you to choose 그래서 or 하지만 for a gap. Here the connector has to be supported by the report: you check what each one claims and what the facts allow.
prerequisites: Knows 그래서, 따라서, 그러므로, 하지만, 그럼에도
Can read short news-style sentences with numbers and percentages
Knows -았/었지만
material:
A news report gives these facts (all true):
① 학교가 급식 시간을 20분에서 30분으로 늘렸다.
② 줄 서는 시간이 평균 12분에서 7분으로 줄었다. 보도는 급식 시간 연장이 그 이유라고 밝혔다 (the report says the longer lunch time is the reason).
③ 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다. 보도는 그 이유를 밝히지 않았다 (the report gives no reason for this).

A student summarises the report:
1. 학교는 급식 시간을 20분에서 30분으로 늘렸다.
2. 그래서 줄 서는 시간이 평균 12분에서 7분으로 줄었다.
3. 그래서 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
4. 이처럼 급식 시간을 늘렸지만 학생 만족도는 오르지 않았다.

steps.prompt: Which sentence uses a connector that claims more than the report says?
lines: 그래서 줄 서는 시간이 평균 12분에서 7분으로 줄었다.
이처럼 급식 시간을 늘렸지만 학생 만족도는 오르지 않았다.
steps.explain: Line 3 uses 그래서, which says the drop in satisfaction is a result of what came before. The report gives no reason for the drop, and a shorter queue is not an obvious cause of lower satisfaction. Line 2 is supported: the report says the longer lunch time is the reason for the shorter queue. Line 4 uses 지만 for contrast, which fits the facts.
hints: For each 그래서, ask: does the report say that the first fact is the reason for the second?
Look at ② and ③ in the facts and compare what each says about the reason.

steps.prompt: Which connectors could replace 그래서 in line 3 without claiming more than the report says? Choose all that apply.

options.text: 따라서 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
options.reveals: Marks the drop as a conclusion that follows from the line before.

options.text: 그럼에도 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
options.reveals: Contrasts the drop with the improvement before.

options.text: 그러므로 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
options.reveals: Makes the drop a result, like 그래서.

options.text: 하지만 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
options.reveals: Contrasts the drop with the improvement before.

options.text: 그런데도 학생 만족도는 62%에서 55%로 낮아졌다.
options.reveals: Says the drop happened despite the improvement.

steps.explain: 그럼에도, 하지만 and 그런데도 show contrast without claiming a cause. 따라서 and 그러므로 claim a result, like 그래서, which the report does not support.
hints: Sort the connectors into those that say 'as a result' and those that say 'in spite of'.
Keep the ones that make no claim about the reason.

acceptable.reason: Valid but incomplete: 그런데도 also works.
Valid but incomplete: 하지만 also works.
Valid but incomplete: 그럼에도 also works.

steps.prompt: Here is a different report: 버스 요금을 1,500원에서 1,200원으로 내렸다. 하루 이용객은 8,000명으로 그대로였다. Write these two facts in Korean as two connected sentences, with a connector that does not claim a cause.

checks.label: has a contrast connector (그럼에도, 그런데도, 하지만, -지만 ...)
does not use a result connector

selfAssess: Did I join the two facts with a contrast, not a result?
Are the numbers from the report in my sentences?
Could a reader think I am claiming that one fact caused the other?

modelAnswers.text: 버스 요금을 1,500원에서 1,200원으로 내렸다. 그럼에도 하루 이용객은 8,000명으로 그대로였다.
버스 요금을 1,500원에서 1,200원으로 내렸지만 하루 이용객은 8,000명으로 그대로였다.

badAnswers.text: 버스 요금을 내렸다. 그래서 이용객이 그대로였다.
badAnswers.why: A result connector, which claims a cause the report does not give.
Only one of the two facts and no connector.

steps.humanReview: Whether the connector fits the meaning and the sentences read naturally in news style.
hints: Write the fare fact first, then the rider fact.
Think of the rider fact as unexpected after the fare fact.

rubric.full: Names line 3 and says the report gives no reason for the drop
Keeps the three contrast connectors and rejects the two result connectors
A contrast connector with both facts
rubric.partial: A connector that fits but one fact is missing

alternatives: Plain additions such as 그리고 are also faithful, but they lose the contrast the facts suggest.
In s2, a student who chooses only two of the contrast connectors is valid but incomplete.
hardCases: Some readers feel that the shorter queue might lower satisfaction (less time to eat?). That is possible but the report does not say it, and the task asks for what the report supports.
'Despite' connectors also imply an expectation. Here the expectation is that an improvement would raise satisfaction.

cautions.language: 그래서, 따라서 and 그러므로 mark a result (the last two are more formal); 그럼에도 and 그런데도 mean 'in spite of that'; 하지만 only contrasts. Learners often treat them as interchangeable.
cautions.culture: A school lunch report is a common news topic; the school and the figures are invented.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Percentages are read aloud as 육십이 퍼센트 (62%) and 오십오 퍼센트 (55%).

auto: Surface checks of s3 (a contrast connector, both facts, no result connector)
human: Whether the connector and the sentences are natural and faithful to the facts
